entry.title: [law] SCOTUS rules unanimously that pension actuaries may use current interest rates when calculating employer withdrawal liability
entry.summary: The Supreme Court unanimously held in M&K Employee Solutions v. IAM National Pension Fund that ERISA actuaries calculating an employer's multiemployer pension withdrawal liability may use current interest-rate assumptions rather than rates locked to the prior plan-year measurement date.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court unanimously held in M&K Employee Solutions v. IAM National Pension Fund that ERISA actuaries calculating an employer's multiemployer pension withdrawal liability may use current interest-rate assumptions rather than rates locked to the prior plan-year measurement date.

The case arose when M&K Employee Solutions withdrew from the IAM National Pension Fund in 2018, triggering a withdrawal liability calculation under the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act. The fund's actuary applied a 6.5% interest rate adopted in January 2018 — after the December 31, 2017 measurement date — rather than the 7.5% rate in effect at year-end. That single percentage-point difference increased M&K's withdrawal liability by $4.36 million, roughly tripling its expected exit bill. M&K sued, arguing ERISA's statutory scheme required actuaries to freeze all assumptions as of the measurement date. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, writing for a unanimous Court, drew a critical distinction: factual plan data must be fixed at the measurement date, but actuarial assumptions are "predictive judgments" and calculation tools — not historical facts about the plan — and therefore can legitimately reflect current economic conditions selected after the measurement date. The ruling resolves a circuit split that had produced inconsistent withdrawal liability calculations across jurisdictions, particularly in New York federal courts.

Why it matters: Employers considering exit from troubled multiemployer pension plans must now account for the reality that actuaries have full discretion to apply whichever interest-rate assumptions are in effect when withdrawal liability is actually calculated — not when the withdrawal occurred. This gives pension funds a structural advantage: by delaying calculations during periods when interest rates are falling, actuaries can significantly inflate withdrawal liability bills, because lower discount rates increase the present value of projected future pension obligations. The ruling is likely to accelerate employer departures from multiemployer plans in sectors with struggling funds — construction, trucking, entertainment — since exit costs become harder to predict and potentially far higher than anticipated at the time of withdrawal. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, which insures multiemployer plans covering approximately 10 million American workers, will need to assess whether the flexibility this ruling permits creates perverse incentives for fund administrators to time calculations strategically. Congress may revisit the Multiemployer Pension Reform Act's withdrawal liability framework in response, particularly as several large funds remain on track for insolvency within the decade.

entry.title: [law] Legislation introduced to require Supreme Court to explain shadow-docket emergency orders within 7 days, as Justice Jackson warns of eroding legitimacy
entry.summary: Representative Jamie Raskin introduced legislation requiring the Supreme Court to publicly justify all emergency shadow-docket orders within seven days, as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warned that unexplained judicial interventions are eroding public confidence in the judiciary at a politically sensitive moment.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Representative Jamie Raskin introduced legislation requiring the Supreme Court to publicly justify all emergency shadow-docket orders within seven days, as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warned that unexplained judicial interventions are eroding public confidence in the judiciary at a politically sensitive moment.

The shadow docket refers to the Supreme Court's practice of deciding high-stakes emergency applications — on abortion access, immigration enforcement, voting rules, and environmental regulation — through unsigned, often one-sentence orders issued without full briefing or oral argument. Raskin's bill would mandate that the Court publish written legal justification within seven days whenever it acts on emergency applications, creating a transparency window that currently does not exist. Justice Jackson became the Court's most vocal internal critic of the practice after the Court shortened the standard 32-day waiting period before finalizing its Voting Rights Act ruling this term — a deviation from established practice that Jackson said occurs "only two or three times in roughly 25 years." Jackson has proposed two structural remedies: establishing a genuine-urgency threshold before the Court intervenes in lower-court cases, and reordering the factors the Court applies when weighing emergency relief. She argued publicly that "courts don't lose authority when they explain themselves — that's where their legitimacy comes from."

Why it matters: The shadow docket has become the primary mechanism through which the current Court's emergency interventions effectively set national policy — often in ways that are difficult for lower courts to apply as precedent and difficult for litigants to challenge. Raskin's bill, if enacted, would be the most significant structural constraint on the Court's emergency powers since Congress reformed the certiorari process in 1925; even without passing, it raises the political cost of unexplained orders. For litigants in high-stakes federal cases — reproductive rights plaintiffs, immigration detainees, environmental regulators — the shadow docket is frequently the decisive forum, making transparency reform more consequential than any single merits ruling. Jackson's public criticism is unusually direct for a sitting justice and signals a level of institutional concern that is rare in the Court's modern history. The reform push has bipartisan resonance: conservative litigants challenging Biden-era regulations were themselves disadvantaged by shadow-docket orders that paused rules without explanation, suggesting the critique transcends partisan interest. Future justices who face a transparency obligation will be incentivized to be more selective about granting emergency relief, potentially shifting the Court's role in ongoing political controversies.

entry.title: [cybersecurity] CISA contractor exposed agency AWS keys and CI/CD credentials on public GitHub for months; senators demand classified briefing
entry.summary: A CISA contractor called Nightwing deliberately disabled GitHub's built-in credential-protection systems and published AWS GovCloud keys, CI/CD pipeline tokens, and RSA private keys for CISA systems to a public repository that remained accessible from at least November 2025 until mid-May 2026, with the exposed AWS keys remaining valid for two more days after CISA was notified.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A CISA contractor called Nightwing deliberately disabled GitHub's built-in credential-protection systems and published AWS GovCloud keys, CI/CD pipeline tokens, and RSA private keys for CISA systems to a public repository that remained accessible from at least November 2025 until mid-May 2026, with the exposed AWS keys remaining valid for two more days after CISA was notified.

GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon discovered a public GitHub repository named "Private-CISA" containing roughly 844 MB of data — 498 MB in the active working tree and the remainder in Git history — including AWS workspace credentials, Firefox password stores, RSA private keys granting access to CISA-IT code repositories, Kubernetes configuration files, and plaintext passwords for at least a dozen internal systems. Brian Krebs reported the exposure on May 18, 2026, after which the account was taken offline; however, the AWS GovCloud keys were not revoked until two days after CISA received the notification. The repository was created on November 13, 2025, meaning credentials may have been discoverable via basic GitHub search for over six months. CISA stated "there is no indication that any sensitive data was compromised," but the agency has not disclosed which credentials were active during the exposure window, who may have accessed the repository, or why continuous monitoring systems failed to detect the publication. Government contractor Nightwing, which had administrative access to CISA's code development platform, is identified as the account operator.

Why it matters: This is a profound operational security failure at the federal agency whose central mission is preventing credential exposures across the US government — and it occurred during a period of one-third workforce reductions, budget cuts of hundreds of millions of dollars, and cancellation of key programs including election security initiatives under the current administration. Senator Maggie Hassan submitted 12 specific questions and demanded a classified briefing from Acting Director Nick Andersen by June 5, warning that "adversaries — like China, Russia, and Iran — seek to gain access to and persistence on federal networks." AWS GovCloud keys provide access to classified federal infrastructure; six months of potential exposure gives sophisticated threat actors time to map CISA's internal architecture, identify targets, and establish persistence that would survive a simple credential rotation. The incident exposes a gap in contractor oversight: Nightwing apparently had sufficient privileges to deliberately bypass security controls, raising systemic questions about how agencies vet and monitor contractor actions in sensitive code environments. Congress is likely to respond with legislation mandating minimum security-certification requirements for contractors with administrative access to agency development platforms, potentially as part of the next DHS appropriations cycle.

entry.title: [cybersecurity] GitHub's 3,800 internal repos stolen in Nx Console supply chain attack tracing back to TanStack breach
entry.summary: GitHub confirmed that approximately 3,800 internal repositories were exfiltrated after a poisoned version of the Nx Console VS Code extension — active on the Visual Studio Marketplace for only 18 minutes on May 18, 2026 — harvested developer credentials as part of a cascading supply chain attack by threat group TeamPCP that also compromised OpenAI, Mistral AI, and Grafana Labs.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

GitHub confirmed that approximately 3,800 internal repositories were exfiltrated after a poisoned version of the Nx Console VS Code extension — active on the Visual Studio Marketplace for only 18 minutes on May 18, 2026 — harvested developer credentials as part of a cascading supply chain attack by threat group TeamPCP that also compromised OpenAI, Mistral AI, and Grafana Labs.

The attack originated when TeamPCP compromised a Narwhal Technologies developer's machine via the TanStack npm supply chain attack that had circulated through the npm ecosystem in early May 2026. Exploiting that foothold, TeamPCP published Nx Console version 18.95.0 — a trojanized build of the popular developer tool with 2.2 million VS Code installs — between 12:30 and 12:48 PM UTC on May 18. The malicious extension "looked and behaved like normal Nx Console, but on startup it silently ran a single shell command that downloaded and executed a hidden package," according to OX Security researcher Nir Zadok. The payload harvested credentials from 1Password vaults, Anthropic Claude Code configurations, npm registry tokens, GitHub CLI tokens, and AWS accounts. A GitHub developer who had installed the extension had their GitHub credentials stolen, giving TeamPCP access to CISO Alexis Wales subsequently confirmed exfiltration of approximately 3,800 internal repositories; Wales stated the attack showed no evidence of impact to customer-owned repositories, enterprises, or organizations. TeamPCP demanded at least $50,000 for the stolen source code.

Why it matters: An 18-minute window was sufficient to steal source code from one of the world's largest software development platforms, illustrating that the VS Code Marketplace is the highest-value supply chain attack surface in modern software development: extensions run in developer environments with access to secrets managers, cloud credential stores, and source control tokens — the full set of keys to any organization's infrastructure. The cascading nature of the attack — TanStack breach → Nx Console developer compromise → GitHub credential theft → 3,800-repo exfiltration, with parallel victims including OpenAI and Mistral — demonstrates that supply chain compromises now self-replicate without requiring the attacker to break into each target independently. GitHub's own internal codebase breach raises questions about the integrity of GitHub Actions workflows, security advisory pipelines, and internal tooling trusted by millions of developers globally. The EU's Cyber Resilience Act, which enters force in 2027, will require mandatory code-signing and vulnerability disclosure for software components — requirements that, if already in place, would have made the TanStack-to-Nx chain significantly harder to execute. The attack should accelerate enterprise adoption of just-in-time credential provisioning and developer machine isolation, practices that limit the blast radius of a single compromised endpoint.

entry.title: [tech law] EU's AI Act Digital Omnibus deal extends high-risk AI deadlines 16 months, bans AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery from December 2026
entry.summary: EU negotiators reached a provisional Digital Omnibus agreement on May 7, 2026, pushing the main Annex III high-risk AI compliance deadline back 16 months to December 2027, adding new prohibitions on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery effective December 2026, and granting the EU AI Office exclusive enforcement jurisdiction over AI systems built on general-purpose AI models.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

EU negotiators reached a provisional Digital Omnibus agreement on May 7, 2026, pushing the main Annex III high-risk AI compliance deadline back 16 months to December 2027, adding new prohibitions on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery effective December 2026, and granting the EU AI Office exclusive enforcement jurisdiction over AI systems built on general-purpose AI models.

The package grants significant timeline relief: Annex III high-risk AI obligations (covering AI in healthcare, employment, credit, education, and critical infrastructure) shift from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, a 16-month extension, while Annex I obligations move from August 2027 to August 2028. The timeline extensions respond to industry evidence that mandatory third-party conformity assessments cannot be completed at scale under the original calendar. On prohibitions, the agreement adds a new Article 4a banning AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) or child sexual abuse material, effective December 2, 2026 — a rare substantive expansion of the law's prohibited-use categories. Enforcement jurisdiction over AI systems that integrate general-purpose AI models (GPAIs) — a category covering most commercial deployments of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta models in European products — is concentrated exclusively in the EU AI Office, eliminating the overlapping national-regulator authority that had paralyzed enforcement. Violations of the new Article 25 information-sharing obligations between GPAI providers and downstream deployers now carry fines of up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or €15 million. Formal adoption is expected in June 2026.

Why it matters: The timeline extensions provide meaningful compliance runway for AI developers in regulated sectors, but they also reset the enforcement calendar for patient-safety advocates, employment-discrimination litigants, and credit-access researchers who were expecting legally enforceable protections by mid-2026. The December 2026 NCII prohibition is the AI Act's first expansion of its prohibited-use list since finalization and will be immediately tested: providers who build image-generation systems without adequate safeguards face liability even for unintentional NCII generation, while deployers face liability only for intentional misuse — a split that will drive litigation over where design negligence ends and user abuse begins. Centralizing GPAI enforcement in the AI Office resolves years of jurisdictional ambiguity but concentrates enormous market power at a single institution: the AI Office alone will now assess pre-market conformity for the world's most commercially significant AI systems deployed in Europe. The Cyber Resilience Act and AI Act together are creating a novel European software liability framework where both security and AI-safety failures carry quantified corporate consequences — a structural shift that US-headquartered developers must build into product roadmaps regardless of how US domestic AI regulation evolves. With formal adoption in June and Official Journal publication anticipated in July, the December 2026 NCII ban is weeks away from being legally binding.

entry.title: [tech law] Supreme Court's pending Chatrie ruling could set the broadest Fourth Amendment digital-privacy limits since Carpenter, covering geofence and reverse-keyword warrants
entry.summary: The Supreme Court's pending ruling in Chatrie v. United States — the first major digital Fourth Amendment case since Carpenter in 2018 — will determine whether law enforcement can compel Google to expose location data on every person within 150 meters of a crime scene without individualized suspicion, with potential implications for reverse-keyword searches and all cloud-stored personal data.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court's pending ruling in Chatrie v. United States — the first major digital Fourth Amendment case since Carpenter in 2018 — will determine whether law enforcement can compel Google to expose location data on every person within 150 meters of a crime scene without individualized suspicion, with potential implications for reverse-keyword searches and all cloud-stored personal data.

Okello Chatrie was identified and convicted of robbing a Virginia credit union after police obtained a geofence warrant directing Google to disclose location records for all 19 accounts tied to devices within 150 meters of the bank during a 30-minute window — a search covering thousands of innocent users' data to identify one suspect. At oral argument in April 2026, liberal justices expressed alarm about searches lacking individualized suspicion across millions of user accounts, while conservative justices invoked the third-party doctrine of Smith v. Maryland (1979), arguing users voluntarily expose location data to Google when they accept its privacy policies. The Court last addressed digital privacy in Carpenter v. United States (2018), holding that seven days of historical cell-site location data required a warrant — but the justices have not yet defined whether Carpenter's reasoning extends to shorter timeframes, different data types, or location data stored by commercial cloud services rather than cell carriers. Petitioner's counsel argued that "anonymity is quite illusory" because location patterns reveal identity without ever needing a name, and that Google updates location records every two minutes within three meters of accuracy.

Why it matters: If the Court upholds geofence warrants, law enforcement in all 50 states will have clear authority to query Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Meta's location databases for everyone present near any crime scene, without naming a suspect in advance — a practice Google received roughly 60,000 requests per year to support as of 2024. Privacy advocates warn the ruling could also authorize "reverse-keyword searches" directing tech companies to identify every user who searched a particular term, and broad cloud sweeps of photos, emails, and documents stored across consumer services. A ruling against geofence warrants would force law enforcement to develop alternative investigative techniques, likely triggering legislation codifying the ruling's limits and defining what warrant particularity requirements apply to bulk cloud data requests. The case has attracted nearly 30 amicus briefs from tech companies, civil liberties organizations, and law enforcement groups — an unusually wide field that signals the ruling will reshape digital investigative practice for a generation. The decision is expected before the Court's term ends in late June 2026, making it one of the most consequential pending privacy rulings of the decade.

entry.title: [global politics] Turkish court annuls CHP leadership election, ousting Özgür Özel and reinstating Kılıçdaroğlu — Borsa Istanbul drops 6%
entry.summary: An Ankara court annulled Turkey's main opposition CHP party's November 2023 leadership congress on May 22, 2026, removing Özgür Özel as party leader and reinstating defeated former chair Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, triggering a 6% crash in Borsa Istanbul and a CHP declaration that the ruling was an "attempted coup."
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

An Ankara court annulled Turkey's main opposition CHP party's November 2023 leadership congress on May 22, 2026, removing Özgür Özel as party leader and reinstating defeated former chair Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, triggering a 6% crash in Borsa Istanbul and a CHP declaration that the ruling was an "attempted coup."

The Republican People's Party (CHP) is Turkey's oldest secular party and currently polls roughly neck-and-neck with President Erdoğan's AKP — the first credible opposition parity in over two decades. The court's ruling centered on allegations that Özel secured delegates' loyalty at the 2023 congress through job promises and other kickbacks when he defeated Kılıçdaroğlu; the CHP denies all charges and characterizes the case as politically motivated. The ruling is part of a broader judicial crackdown on the CHP since 2024 that has resulted in the detention of hundreds of party members and elected officials. Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu — widely seen as Erdoğan's most formidable political rival and the CHP's 2028 presidential candidate — has been imprisoned for over a year on charges including insulting public officials, charges the party says are fabricated. The appeals court decision effectively reinstalls Kılıçdaroğlu, who lost the 2023 presidential election to Erdoğan, as interim party chair — restoring a figure seen by many within the CHP as a weaker, more divisive leader — while the pro-Kurdish DEM Party called the ruling "a black stain on Turkish democracy."

Why it matters: A court voiding the internal election of a legally registered opposition party and installing leadership of its choice represents a direct assault on the organizational autonomy that multiparty democracy requires; if sustained, it eliminates the CHP's ability to choose its own leadership free of judicial interference aligned with the ruling government. The 6% Borsa Istanbul drop and government bond decline reflect investor concern that political instability will deepen under a manufactured leadership crisis, especially at a time when Turkey's central bank is relying on institutional credibility to manage persistent inflation. The CHP's vow to "resist" the ruling raises the prospect of street protests that could further destabilize the country ahead of the 2028 presidential election, which Erdoğan is constitutionally barred from contesting unless he engineers a constitutional referendum or calls early elections. For the European Union — which periodically conditions Turkey's EU candidate status on democratic governance standards — the ruling provides fresh grounds for those arguing that accession talks should be formally suspended. The imprisonment of İmamoğlu already produced a market shock earlier in 2025; a second leadership destabilization suggests the government is systematically neutralizing opposition capacity ahead of the next electoral cycle regardless of international reaction.

entry.title: [global politics] WHO raises Ebola risk to 'very high' in DR Congo — 177 suspected deaths, no approved vaccine for Bundibugyo strain
entry.summary: The WHO upgraded the Ebola risk in eastern DR Congo to "very high" at the national level on May 22, 2026, five days after declaring a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, as nearly 750 suspected cases and 177 suspected deaths dwarf the 82 confirmed cases — a gap that officials warn indicates an outbreak far larger than detection systems are capturing, with no licensed vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The WHO upgraded the Ebola risk in eastern DR Congo to "very high" at the national level on May 22, 2026, five days after declaring a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, as nearly 750 suspected cases and 177 suspected deaths dwarf the 82 confirmed cases — a gap that officials warn indicates an outbreak far larger than detection systems are capturing, with no licensed vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain.

The current outbreak involves the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a less common and less studied variant compared to the Zaire strain that drove the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic (11,000 deaths) and the 2018–2020 DRC outbreak that was controlled using ring vaccination. Unlike for Zaire Ebola, no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists for Bundibugyo virus disease, which carries an estimated case fatality rate of 25–30%, eliminating the primary containment strategy used in recent outbreaks. The outbreak is centered in Ituri province in eastern DRC — an area experiencing active armed conflict, mass displacement, and deep community mistrust — conditions that severely impede contact tracing, safe burial protocols, and treatment-center operations. WHO's May 17 PHEIC declaration followed confirmed cases in Kampala, Uganda, among travelers from DRC, and sporadic cases in Germany, the Czech Republic, and the Netherlands. Provincial authorities in Ituri imposed funeral restrictions and gathering limits of 50 people, but residents in Rwampara burned a treatment center amid misinformation-fueled unrest, and a high positivity rate among initial samples — 8 positive among 13 collected — suggests widespread undetected transmission.

Why it matters: The Bundibugyo variant's lack of approved medical countermeasures transforms what would otherwise be a containable outbreak into a race between traditional epidemiological tools — isolation, contact tracing, safe burials — and a highly lethal virus spreading through one of the world's most operationally difficult environments. The WHO Regional Director's unusual public warning that "it would be a big mistake to underestimate" the Bundibugyo strain signals that health authorities believe the confirmed case count is a severe underestimate, and that the outbreak's true scale may require a response on the order of the 2018–2020 effort that ultimately involved over $1 billion in international funding. Spread to Uganda and three European countries via air travel demonstrates that Ituri's porous borders and ongoing displacement make geographic containment unreliable; the international community cannot wait for DRC to control the outbreak domestically before preparing port-of-entry screening and healthcare surge capacity. Emergency Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates exist in research pipelines, but regulatory timelines make approval within the current outbreak window unlikely without coordinated emergency use authorization from multiple national agencies — a process that required months even during COVID. For international health governance under post-COVID reform proposals, the Bundibugyo outbreak is the first major test of whether accelerated countermeasure development pipelines and early-warning systems have been meaningfully improved since 2022.

entry.content:
law

The Supreme Court rescheduled its conference on Trump's petition challenging the E. Jean Carroll $5 million sexual assault verdict for the eleventh consecutive time since January 2026, without public explanation — an extraordinary delay that likely reflects coordination with a parallel Carroll defamation petition Trump plans to file, in which he may again attempt to substitute the federal government as defendant under the Westfall Act, a theory that would extinguish the existing judgment on procedural grounds.

tech_law

CISA announced a formal nomination portal allowing security researchers and vendors to submit candidates for its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, replacing informal email channels; organizations that patch KEV-listed bugs remediate 3.5× faster than for unlisted vulnerabilities, and CISA is considering cutting mandatory patch windows from three weeks to three days for AI-accelerated high-severity threats. UK regulator Ofcom required six platforms to implement child-protection changes by April 2026 under the Online Safety Act, securing commitments from Meta (AI detection of sexualized DMs, hiding teen connection lists), Snapchat (restricting adult-child contact), and Roblox (parental messaging controls), while publicly declaring YouTube and TikTok "still not safe enough" — with 10-percent-of-global-revenue fines available if platforms fail to comply. Two Americans — Adam Young and Harrison Gevirtz of C.A. Cloud Attribution — pleaded guilty to supplying phone numbers and call-routing infrastructure to India-based tech-support fraud centers that targeted elderly and disabled Americans from 2016 to 2022, continuing even after receiving law-enforcement complaints in 2017; sentencing is set for June 16.

global_politics

Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao told a Senate panel Thursday that the $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan has been put on "pause" to preserve munitions for Operation Epic Fury against Iran, a disclosure amplified by Trump's statements that the sale was discussed with Xi Jinping at the May 14 Beijing summit and could serve as a "negotiating chip" — a break from decades of policy against consulting Beijing on Taiwan arms. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced an October 19 referendum asking voters whether to pursue a binding independence vote, after separatists submitted over 300,000 signatures; however, an Alberta court ruled the process unconstitutional for failing to consult First Nations, and roughly 30 percent of Albertans poll in favor of separation. Iran's Supreme National Security Council established a formal Persian Gulf Strait Authority empowered to collect passage fees — some ships have reportedly already paid up to $2 million per transit — directly defying UNCLOS's transit passage provisions for international straits, prompting the US and China to jointly declare Hormuz must remain open at their Beijing summit.

tech

Jacob Butler (alias "Dort"), a 23-year-old Ottawa resident, was arrested and faces charges in both Canada and the United States for operating Kimwolf, an IoT DDoS-for-hire botnet that reached nearly 30 terabits per second in attack volume, issued over 25,000 attack commands, and caused losses exceeding $1 million for individual victims; authorities simultaneously seized three competing botnets — Aisuru, JackSkid, and Mossad — in a coordinated infrastructure takedown.

entry.title: [global politics] US acting navy secretary says $14bn Taiwan arms sale put on pause to preserve munitions for Iran war
entry.summary: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told a Senate panel Thursday that the US has paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan to ensure sufficient munitions are available for the ongoing Iran war operation known as Epic Fury.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told a Senate panel Thursday that the US has paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan to ensure sufficient munitions are available for the ongoing Iran war operation known as Epic Fury.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified before the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense on May 22 that the authorized $14 billion foreign military sale package to Taiwan — which includes advanced missiles and munitions central to Taiwan's layered defense — has been placed on "pause" to preserve stockpiles for Operation Epic Fury, the ongoing US military campaign against Iran. Cao said the administration has "plenty" of munitions for the Iran operation and promised the Taiwan sale would resume once the administration decided. The announcement followed Trump's May 14 Beijing summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, where Trump stated the Taiwan sale was on the table and suggested it could function as a "negotiating chip" — a direct break from four decades of US policy against consulting Beijing on Taiwan arms decisions under the Taiwan Relations Act. Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai publicly urged Washington to continue the sales as essential for regional stability, while Crisis Group analyst William Yang warned the pause will "exacerbate anxiety and skepticism about US support in Taiwan" and make it politically difficult for Taipei to seek additional defense budget authorizations. The Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 requires the US government to provide Taiwan with "defense articles and defense services in such quantity as may be necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capability," a statutory obligation now in tension with Pentagon readiness demands.

Why it matters: If the US treats a legally mandated arms sale as a diplomatic concession tradeable with China — Beijing's single most emphasized red line — it signals a structural shift in America's deterrence commitment that China's military planners, who have spent decades studying US Indo-Pacific readiness gaps, will immediately register. The public disclosure of insufficient munitions production capacity to sustain simultaneous operations in the Middle East and the Pacific is a strategic intelligence gift: it confirms what was previously only estimated about America's two-theater problem. For Taiwan's defense establishment, the message is that US supply cannot be relied upon when American operational priorities compete — accelerating investment in domestic weapons production and alternative suppliers. Congressional hawks are likely to respond with legislation establishing mandatory floor-level arms delivery timelines that constrain future executive discretion, which may paradoxically tie the next administration's Taiwan policy more tightly. The Iran war's spillover into Indo-Pacific security commitments represents the most significant US credibility test in the region since the Trump administration's first term.

entry.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced an October 19, 2026 referendum asking voters whether to pursue a binding vote on separating from Canada, after separatists delivered over 300,000 signatures, but a court ruling found the process unconstitutional for failing to consult First Nations.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced an October 19, 2026 referendum asking voters whether to pursue a binding vote on separating from Canada, after separatists delivered over 300,000 signatures, but a court ruling found the process unconstitutional for failing to consult First Nations.

Alberta separatists submitted over 300,000 signatures to provincial authorities — nearly double the 178,000 required for a citizen-led referendum petition — reflecting a surge in alienation from federal policies on climate, equalization payments, and natural resource regulation. Premier Danielle Smith announced the United Conservative Party government would hold an October 19, 2026 referendum with several constitutional questions, including one asking voters whether to pursue a formal binding independence referendum. However, on May 13, Alberta Justice Shaina Leonard issued a significant ruling finding the entire referendum process unconstitutional on the grounds that Alberta's First Nations peoples — whose treaty rights predate Canadian confederation and cover substantial portions of the province — were never consulted, and that separation would violate those treaty rights. Premier Smith announced she will appeal the decision and is considering using executive authority to add independence questions to the October ballot over the court ruling. Current polling shows approximately 30 percent of Alberta residents favor independence, up sharply from pre-2024 levels, driven by anger at federal carbon taxes and what many Albertans perceive as structural economic disadvantage within confederation despite generating roughly 17 percent of Canada's GDP with less than 12 percent of its population.

Why it matters: Alberta's independence movement is the most consequential secessionist crisis Canada has faced since Quebec's 1995 independence referendum, which failed by fewer than 50,000 votes. Alberta controls the majority of Canada's conventional oil and gas production and anchors the Trans Mountain Pipeline system; independence would fracture the Canadian fiscal union and eliminate billions in equalization transfers redistributed annually to other provinces. The First Nations constitutional barrier is substantive rather than procedural — under the Supreme Court of Canada's precedents, Indigenous treaty rights create duties that cannot be overridden by provincial legislation or referenda, and a vote held in defiance of those duties would have no legal standing. For Canada's federal government, aggressively challenging the movement risks inflaming Albertan grievances; offering fiscal concessions risks incentivizing Quebec and other provinces to make similar demands. For international bond markets and energy sector investors, even a credible 30-percent polling figure introduces sovereign risk pricing into long-term Canadian energy infrastructure assets and the Canadian dollar.

entry.title: [global politics] Iran establishes formal Hormuz transit authority to charge ships for passage, directly defying international maritime law
entry.summary: Iran's Supreme National Security Council established a formal Persian Gulf Strait Authority empowered to collect passage fees from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with some vessels reportedly already paying up to $2 million per transit, in direct violation of UNCLOS transit passage rights.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran's Supreme National Security Council established a formal Persian Gulf Strait Authority empowered to collect passage fees from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with some vessels reportedly already paying up to $2 million per transit, in direct violation of UNCLOS transit passage rights.

Iran initially declared the Strait of Hormuz "closed" in March 2026 and threatened military action against ships attempting to pass; it has since institutionalized its control by establishing the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a formal governmental body with a mandate to collect transit fees from commercial vessels, with reports indicating some ships have already paid fees reaching $2 million per transit rather than risk confrontation. The Iranian parliament separately approved the toll regime to enforce Tehran's assertion of "sovereign role" over the strait — a claim directly contradicted by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), under which all nations have the right of "transit passage" through international straits that connect the high seas, with coastal states explicitly prohibited from suspending or charging for such transit. The Strait carries roughly 20 percent of the world's daily oil and LNG supply; the UK has deployed drones, fighter aircraft, and a Royal Navy warship to an international defensive mission protecting commercial shipping in the waterway. At their May 14 Beijing summit, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping issued a joint statement declaring Hormuz must remain open, with China explicitly opposing both militarization and tolls — a significant alignment given China's status as the world's largest buyer of Gulf oil.

Why it matters: Iran's establishment of a permanent governmental transit authority — rather than ad hoc naval interference — creates an institutional mechanism that will persist beyond any ceasefire and sets an internationally dangerous precedent: that a coastal state can impose fees on transit through an international strait by simply constituting a regulatory body. The UNCLOS framework exists precisely to prevent such rent-seeking behavior at maritime chokepoints, and Iran's direct defiance of it challenges the entire rules-based maritime order that enables $4 trillion in annual seaborne trade. China's joint statement against the toll regime is strategically significant: Beijing's interest in unimpeded Gulf oil imports currently outweighs its interest in the precedent Iran's model might set for Chinese claims in the South China Sea — but that calculus could shift. International shipping insurers have already repriced Gulf routes substantially, and any sustained enforcement of the toll regime could permanently redirect trade through alternative routes, changing global refinery investment and LNG terminal location decisions. Watch for the US and European navies to test Iranian enforcement of the toll regime directly, which would force Iran to either back down or escalate into a formal confrontation with legal implications under the law of naval warfare.

entry.title: [cybersecurity] Kimwolf botmaster "Dort" arrested in Canada, charged in US with running 30-Tbps DDoS-for-hire botnet and swatting security researchers
entry.summary: Canadian authorities and the FBI arrested 23-year-old Jacob Butler (alias "Dort") in Ottawa, charging him in both the US and Canada for operating Kimwolf, an IoT botnet that launched DDoS attacks reaching nearly 30 terabits per second and for conducting swatting campaigns against security researchers who exposed it.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Canadian authorities and the FBI arrested 23-year-old Jacob Butler (alias "Dort") in Ottawa, charging him in both the US and Canada for operating Kimwolf, an IoT botnet that launched DDoS attacks reaching nearly 30 terabits per second and for conducting swatting campaigns against security researchers who exposed it.

Jacob Butler, a 23-year-old Ottawa resident operating as "Dort," was arrested by Ontario Provincial Police and now faces criminal charges on both sides of the border: in the United States, aiding and abetting computer intrusion with a maximum 10-year sentence; in Canada, unauthorized computer use and mischief related to computer data. Butler allegedly constructed and operated Kimwolf, malware targeting IoT devices including digital photo frames and web cameras, which he both rented to other cybercriminals as DDoS-for-hire and operated directly, achieving attack volumes of nearly 30 terabits per second — a record at the time — and issuing more than 25,000 attack commands, with individual victim losses exceeding $1 million. On March 19, law enforcement simultaneously dismantled Kimwolf's technical infrastructure and three competing botnets — Aisuru, JackSkid, and Mossad — in a coordinated operation designed to maximize disruption across the DDoS-for-hire market. Beyond the botnet operation, Butler conducted swatting attacks and harassment campaigns against security researchers, including two swatting attempts against Ben Brundage, founder of Synthient, which had publicly disclosed Kimwolf vulnerabilities; Butler was identified through IP address analysis, online account records, payment transaction history, and encrypted messaging data.

Why it matters: The simultaneous takedown of four competing IoT botnets signals a shift in law enforcement strategy: rather than disrupting individual actors sequentially, agencies are targeting the entire DDoS-for-hire ecosystem in coordinated operations that deny the market multiple alternatives at once. The swatting charges against security researchers establish an important precedent — using false emergency reports to terrorize defenders is now treated as a distinct criminal offense alongside the underlying cybercrime, raising the cost of researcher intimidation as a counter-tactic. The dual US-Canada prosecution maximizes sentencing exposure across two legal systems, and the FBI's involvement through Ontario Provincial Police creates a template for cross-border coordination that other nations can replicate against actors who shelter in countries without extradition treaties. For ransomware operators, DDoS extortion groups, and other Kimwolf customers, the infrastructure seizure means both service disruption and the risk that transaction records, attack logs, and communications captured from Kimwolf's servers can now be used to identify and prosecute the downstream criminal ecosystem Butler served.

entry.title: [tech law] CISA opens Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog to external researcher nominations, eyes cutting patch deadlines from three weeks to three days
entry.summary: CISA launched a formal submission portal allowing security researchers, vendors, and industry partners to nominate vulnerabilities for its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, replacing informal email processes, and is considering reducing mandatory federal patch windows from three weeks to three days for AI-accelerated high-severity threats.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

CISA launched a formal submission portal allowing security researchers, vendors, and industry partners to nominate vulnerabilities for its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, replacing informal email processes, and is considering reducing mandatory federal patch windows from three weeks to three days for AI-accelerated high-severity threats.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency announced a new standardized nomination form enabling external security researchers, software vendors, and industry partners to submit candidate vulnerabilities for the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — the primary US government list of bugs confirmed as actively exploited in the wild. The process replaces informal email channels with structured evidence-based submissions requiring documentation of active exploitation, incorporating quality controls intended to prevent false reporting while reducing the delay between researcher discovery and catalog listing. Empirical data shows that organizations remediate vulnerabilities listed on the KEV 3.5 times faster than bugs not on the catalog, making the speed of additions a direct driver of defensive response across both federal agencies and critical infrastructure operators. Former CISA CIO Robert Costello said the standardized process enables "faster KEV additions and, ultimately, faster defensive action across the whole ecosystem." CISA is also reportedly considering reducing mandatory federal patch deadlines from the current three-week window under BOD 22-01 to as little as three days for certain high-severity threats — a potential response to AI-driven acceleration of exploitation timelines, where zero-day weaponization now often occurs within hours of public vulnerability disclosure.

Why it matters: The KEV catalog is the operational backbone of the November 2021 Binding Operational Directive that requires all federal civilian agencies to patch listed vulnerabilities within set deadlines; it is also widely adopted by critical infrastructure operators, state governments, and international allies as the de facto authoritative list of actively exploited bugs. Opening nominations to the broader security community closes the gap between when researchers discover active exploitation and when CISA can verify and publish — currently measured in days to weeks, during which attackers maintain access while defenders wait for confirmation. The potential three-day patch deadline would be transformative for federal IT operations: moving from three weeks to three days requires automated patch pipelines, real-time vulnerability inventory, and testing infrastructure that most agencies currently lack, effectively forcing a modernization investment. For software vendors, the nomination portal creates new due-diligence pressure — failure to proactively report known exploited vulnerabilities will increasingly be treated as a compliance failure. The EU's ENISA and UK's NCSC both maintain parallel catalogs that shadow the KEV; any acceleration of CISA's process will cascade globally, tightening the international patch cycle across allied critical infrastructure.

entry.title: [tech law] UK Ofcom secures child-safety commitments from Meta, Snapchat, and Roblox under Online Safety Act; declares YouTube and TikTok still not safe enough
entry.summary: UK regulator Ofcom required six major platforms to implement child-protection changes by April 2026 under the Online Safety Act, securing commitments from Meta, Snapchat, and Roblox, while publicly declaring YouTube and TikTok "still not safe enough" with 10-percent-of-global-revenue fines available for non-compliance.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

UK regulator Ofcom required six major platforms to implement child-protection changes by April 2026 under the Online Safety Act, securing commitments from Meta, Snapchat, and Roblox, while publicly declaring YouTube and TikTok "still not safe enough" with 10-percent-of-global-revenue fines available for non-compliance.

Ofcom, enforcing the UK Online Safety Act, required six platforms — Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, Roblox, YouTube, and TikTok — to implement specific child safety design changes by end of April 2026. Meta committed to hiding teenagers' connection lists on Instagram by default and to deploying AI systems to detect "likely sexualized conversations" in direct messages before they occur. Snapchat agreed to restrict adult-child contact and eliminate features encouraging connections with unknown users. Roblox committed to allowing parents to disable direct messaging for accounts belonging to users under 16. YouTube and TikTok declined to make significant commitments; Ofcom responded by publicly naming them as platforms that are "still not safe enough" — a calculated naming-and-shaming step that precedes formal enforcement proceedings. The Online Safety Act grants Ofcom the power to impose fines of up to 10 percent of global annual turnover, which would amount to billions of dollars for Meta, TikTok, or YouTube. The UK government simultaneously opened a consultation on whether to restrict social media access for younger teenagers, with conclusions expected in coming months.

Why it matters: YouTube and TikTok's refusal to commit to design changes, even under threat of 10-percent-of-global-revenue fines from a major English-speaking market, will become the test case for whether the UK's Online Safety Act has genuine enforcement teeth or is primarily aspirational. Ofcom's public naming approach — declaring specific platforms unsafe before issuing financial penalties — creates reputational and market pressure independent of the formal fine timeline, a model that regulators in Australia, Canada, and EU member states are watching closely for replication. Meta's acceptance of the AI-detection mandate for sexualized messaging, if implemented at scale, creates a benchmark of technical feasibility that regulators can cite against other platforms claiming such detection is impossible. For EU DSA enforcement, the UK approach is diverging deliberately: Brussels focuses on algorithmic transparency and content moderation systems while London targets specific product design features that enable grooming, generating two distinct but complementary regulatory frameworks that platforms must satisfy simultaneously. The consultation on age-based access restrictions signals a potential move toward mandatory age verification — legislation that would directly challenge the technical and privacy architecture of every major social platform operating in the UK.

entry.title: [law] Supreme Court postpones decision on Trump petition challenging Carroll $5M verdict for the eleventh consecutive conference
entry.summary: The Supreme Court rescheduled its conference on whether to accept Donald Trump's petition challenging a jury's $5 million verdict for E. Jean Carroll for the eleventh time since January 2026, without public explanation, in a procedural delay that analysts link to anticipated parallel litigation over a related Carroll defamation judgment.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court rescheduled its conference on whether to accept Donald Trump's petition challenging a jury's $5 million verdict for E. Jean Carroll for the eleventh time since January 2026, without public explanation, in a procedural delay that analysts link to anticipated parallel litigation over a related Carroll defamation judgment.

Writer E. Jean Carroll sued Trump in 2022 alleging he sexually assaulted her in a Bergdorf Goodman dressing room in 1996 and subsequently defamed her through social media statements. A Manhattan federal jury in May 2023 awarded Carroll $5 million; the Second Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed. Trump petitioned the Supreme Court in November 2025 seeking certiorari — discretionary review — challenging the trial court's admission of testimony from other women who alleged similar assaults by Trump and the "Access Hollywood" audio recording as prior-bad-act evidence. The Court has now rescheduled the conference at which justices would vote on whether to accept the petition eleven times since January 2026, providing no public explanation for each postponement; the vast majority of cert petitions are resolved at one or two conferences. Observers believe the delays are coordinated with a separate Carroll defamation case in which Trump is expected to petition the Court and again attempt to have the Department of Justice substituted as defendant under the Westfall Act — arguing his post-presidency statements constituted official presidential conduct and should trigger sovereign immunity, a theory that would extinguish the existing judgment on procedural grounds rather than the merits.

Why it matters: Eleven consecutive conference postponements without explanation are procedurally extraordinary and suggest either deep division among justices about whether to take the case or deliberate coordination with the forthcoming defamation petition — possibly to consolidate both Carroll cases for a single grant-or-deny decision. If the Court accepts the evidentiary challenge to prior-bad-act testimony, it would have transformative implications for civil sexual assault litigation across the federal courts, potentially restricting the tools plaintiffs use to establish patterns of conduct. The Westfall Act substitution theory — if the Court ever accepted it — would be constitutionally momentous: it would establish that a president's public statements about pending private lawsuits are "official acts," extending immunity in a way no prior court has recognized while eliminating the Carroll judgment on purely procedural grounds. The absence of any public explanation for each postponement has intensified criticism that the Court's opacity on cert procedure enables the appearance of political coordination, feeding the broader transparency critique Justice Jackson has advanced in recent public remarks. The final resolution — whether a grant or denial — is now expected only after Trump files the anticipated defamation petition, likely by late June 2026.

entry.summary: Adam Young and Harrison Gevirtz, operators of C.A. Cloud Attribution, pleaded guilty to supplying phone numbers and call-routing services to India-based tech-support fraud centers from 2016 to 2022, continuing even after receiving law-enforcement complaints in 2017, and face up to three years in prison at sentencing on June 16.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Adam Young and Harrison Gevirtz, operators of C.A. Cloud Attribution, pleaded guilty to supplying phone numbers and call-routing services to India-based tech-support fraud centers from 2016 to 2022, continuing even after receiving law-enforcement complaints in 2017, and face up to three years in prison at sentencing on June 16.

Adam Young, 42, and Harrison Gevirtz, 33, co-operators of C.A. Cloud Attribution, pleaded guilty to misprision of a felony — knowingly concealing and failing to report a felony — for providing telephone numbers, call routing, and call-forwarding infrastructure to India-based tech-support scam operations from 2016 to 2022. The scam centers targeted elderly and disabled Americans with fake malware warnings, routing them to call centers in India where fraudsters pressured victims into paying hundreds of dollars for worthless technical support services; operators then exploited remote device access to steal additional financial information. Young and Gevirtz continued supplying services even after receiving law-enforcement complaints about the scam operations in 2017 and took active steps to help fraudsters evade detection. Department of Justice prosecutors emphasized that the pair's continued service with actual knowledge of the fraud distinguishes this from ordinary negligent provision of telecommunications infrastructure. The two defendants face up to three years in prison at a sentencing hearing scheduled for June 16.

Why it matters: This prosecution is part of a deliberate DOJ strategy to hold US-based "infrastructure enablers" accountable for the full downstream harm of transnational fraud schemes — a significant evolution beyond the traditional approach of pursuing only the foreign call-center operators themselves, who are often beyond the reach of US extradition. Tech-support fraud targeting elderly Americans generates an estimated $1 billion in annual losses; prosecuting domestic choke points — phone number provisioners, payment processors, virtual private server providers — disrupts whole ecosystems rather than individual operatives who can be replaced within days. The guilty plea to "misprision of a felony" rather than conspiracy suggests prosecutors prioritized quick cooperation and information from both defendants, who may serve as witnesses in future cross-border proceedings against Indian call-center operators. For VoIP providers and telecommunications infrastructure companies, the case establishes a binding standard: knowledge of ongoing fraud combined with continued service provision is now a federal criminal exposure, creating a strong incentive to cut off suspicious customers immediately rather than wait for formal law-enforcement demands. Watch for DOJ to use the cooperation obtained here to bring charges against at least one India-based call center principal before the June 16 sentencing date, as leverage over Young and Gevirtz to produce maximum cooperation.

entry.title: [law] Supreme Court rules 8-1 against cruise lines in Cuban confiscation case, exposing them to $400M+ in Helms-Burton Act damages
entry.summary: The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in Havana Docks Corp. v. Royal Caribbean that four major cruise lines incurred Helms-Burton Act liability by transporting nearly one million passengers through Cuba's confiscated Havana cruise terminal between 2016 and 2019.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in Havana Docks Corp. v. Royal Caribbean that four major cruise lines incurred Helms-Burton Act liability by transporting nearly one million passengers through Cuba's confiscated Havana cruise terminal between 2016 and 2019.

Havana Docks Corporation held the rights to operate Havana's cruise port terminal until the Cuban government confiscated the property in 1960. The 1996 Helms-Burton Act allows U.S. nationals to sue anyone "trafficking in property confiscated by the Cuban Government," but presidents continuously suspended the lawsuit provision from 1996 until 2019, when President Trump declined renewal. Between 2016 and 2019, four cruise lines — Royal Caribbean, Norwegian, Carnival, and MSC — transported nearly one million passengers through the docks, generating substantial revenue. A Miami federal district court awarded Havana Docks over $400 million in damages; the Eleventh Circuit reversed 2-1. In an opinion by Justice Clarence Thomas joined by seven colleagues, the Court held that "confiscated property" encompasses both the physical docks and all prior interests in them, and that any use of such tainted property triggers liability to those holding those interests. Justices Sotomayor and Kavanaugh wrote separately to flag concerns about unlimited recovery possibilities. Justice Elena Kagan was the sole dissenter, arguing that Havana Docks' expired leasehold interest should not qualify for recovery.

Why it matters: The ruling significantly expands potential liability for businesses that have conducted commercial operations using formerly private Cuban assets. With hundreds of billions of dollars in confiscated Cuban property potentially qualifying for claims, the decision could ultimately affect cruise operators, hotel chains, energy companies, and any enterprise that has used assets seized since 1959. The 8-1 majority signals that Helms-Burton trafficking claims are to be read broadly — a major win for Cuban exile claimants and a significant compliance warning for global companies with current or historical Cuba operations. The case returns to lower courts for the cruise lines to raise remaining defenses, including damages-calculation arguments that will determine whether the $400 million award is ultimately reinstated. For legal and compliance officers, the ruling creates new due-diligence obligations before conducting Cuba-related commercial activity and may affect operations in other jurisdictions with comparable confiscation histories.

entry.title: [law] Supreme Court dismisses death-row IQ dispute 5-4, leaving Alabama inmate's Eighth Amendment intellectual disability protection intact
entry.summary: The Supreme Court dismissed Hamm v. Smith 5-4 as improvidently granted, leaving intact the Eleventh Circuit ruling that Alabama death-row inmate Joseph Smith is intellectually disabled under Atkins v. Virginia and cannot be executed.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court dismissed Hamm v. Smith 5-4 as improvidently granted, leaving intact the Eleventh Circuit ruling that Alabama death-row inmate Joseph Smith is intellectually disabled under Atkins v. Virginia and cannot be executed.

Joseph Smith has been on Alabama's death row for over 20 years following his 1997 conviction for the robbery and murder of Durk Van Dam. Across multiple proceedings, Smith obtained five IQ test scores ranging from 72 to 78 — a borderline range at the center of a circuit dispute over how courts must handle multiple IQ results in Atkins claims. The 2001 Atkins v. Virginia ruling bars execution of intellectually disabled persons under the Eighth Amendment, but lower courts have disagreed on whether to average scores or credit the lowest reading. Alabama argued courts must consider the cumulative weight of all scores; the Eleventh Circuit ruled against Alabama and found Smith intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the question but dismissed the case as "improvidently granted" — meaning at least five justices concluded it should not have been accepted — leaving the Eleventh Circuit ruling in Smith's favor undisturbed. Justice Sotomayor filed a 22-page concurrence explaining the dismissal; Justice Alito dissented in 24 pages joined by Thomas, Roberts, and Gorsuch, warning the dismissal will produce inconsistent outcomes across circuits.

Why it matters: The dismissal delivers an immediate practical victory for Smith, whose execution had been pending resolution, and represents a significant moment in the ongoing tension between the conservative majority and liberal bloc on capital punishment. Alito's pointed dissent predicts that future borderline-IQ cases will be decided inconsistently across circuits and signals that the right-wing justices view current Atkins doctrine as too permissive — meaning the issue is likely to return to the Court in a future case. For capital defense attorneys, the ruling preserves a favorable framework for establishing intellectual disability through IQ score ranges without requiring a single definitive test result. The dismissal also reflects the Court's broader pattern of accepting high-profile constitutional questions and then retreating before issuing a ruling. Courts in the Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits handling similar borderline-IQ cases will now navigate conflicting precedents without Supreme Court guidance.

entry.title: [law] NY Court of Appeals holds Justice for Injured Workers Act retroactive, blocking use of WCB rulings to defeat construction injury suits
entry.summary: New York's Court of Appeals held in Garcia v. Monadnock Construction (2026 NY Slip Op 03217) that the Justice for Injured Workers Act applies retroactively to all pending cases, barring defendants from using prior Workers' Compensation Board determinations as collateral estoppel to dismiss personal injury claims.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

New York's Court of Appeals held in Garcia v. Monadnock Construction (2026 NY Slip Op 03217) that the Justice for Injured Workers Act applies retroactively to all pending cases, barring defendants from using prior Workers' Compensation Board determinations as collateral estoppel to dismiss personal injury claims.

Plaintiff Waldy Quinones Garcia sustained neck and back injuries in a construction site accident on August 6, 2020, filing both a civil personal injury lawsuit and a workers' compensation claim. A Workers' Compensation Board panel denied his claim in October 2021, finding no causal relationship to the accident. The construction defendants moved for summary judgment, seeking to use that WCB ruling as collateral estoppel to foreclose Garcia's civil suit. The Justice for Injured Workers Act (JIWA), enacted as L 2022, ch 835 and effective December 30, 2022, created Workers' Compensation Law sections 11(2) and 118-a, explicitly barring courts from giving collateral estoppel effect to WCB findings in civil personal injury actions. Lower courts split on whether JIWA reached accidents and WCB proceedings predating the statute's enactment. The Court of Appeals resolved the split, holding JIWA applies retroactively to all pending cases, and ruled the defendants' collateral estoppel defense was "palpably insufficient and devoid of merit" — requiring denial of their summary judgment motion.

Why it matters: This ruling is significant for New York personal injury practice, especially construction injury cases under Labor Law sections 200, 240, and 241. Before JIWA, employers and insurers routinely obtained favorable WCB causation rulings in administrative proceedings where injured workers often had minimal representation, then used those findings to defeat civil lawsuits, effectively letting an administrative system determine tort liability. JIWA was designed to sever that pathway, but its retroactive reach had been contested across hundreds of pending cases. By holding JIWA fully retroactive, the Court of Appeals has revived injury claims defendants sought to extinguish and restored injured workers' right to have causation decided by a civil jury. For defense counsel and insurers, the ruling eliminates a reliable early-exit summary judgment tool; for plaintiffs' attorneys, it reopens previously dismissed cases. Any dismissals on collateral estoppel grounds issued between JIWA's December 2022 enactment and today may be subject to reinstatement motions, potentially generating a significant wave of renewed litigation across New York state courts.

entry.title: [global politics] Paris appeals court convicts Air France and Airbus of manslaughter in the 2009 AF447 crash, reversing acquittal in France's worst aviation disaster
entry.summary: The Paris Court of Appeal found Air France and Airbus solely and entirely responsible for the June 2009 crash of flight AF447 that killed all 228 aboard, reversing a 2023 acquittal and imposing the maximum corporate manslaughter fine of 225,000 euros per passenger.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Paris Court of Appeal found Air France and Airbus solely and entirely responsible for the June 2009 crash of flight AF447 that killed all 228 aboard, reversing a 2023 acquittal and imposing the maximum corporate manslaughter fine of 225,000 euros per passenger.

Flight AF447 departed Rio de Janeiro on June 1, 2009, bound for Paris with 216 passengers and 12 crew. Over the mid-Atlantic, a storm caused the aircraft's pitot tubes — sensors measuring airspeed — to ice over; receiving conflicting speed readings, pilots responded by climbing, causing the plane to stall and plunge into the ocean. Recovery of the black boxes required two years of deep-sea salvage. A Paris criminal court acquitted both companies in 2023, accepting the defense that pilot error was the proximate cause. Prosecutors appealed, and the Paris Court of Appeal reversed on May 21, 2026, finding both companies fully responsible. The court found Air France failed to provide adequate high-altitude stall recovery training — a deficiency the carrier acknowledged — and that Airbus had not addressed known pitot tube icing defects with sufficient urgency despite earlier safety alerts. The maximum corporate manslaughter penalty is 225,000 euros per victim; prosecutors described the total fines as largely symbolic given the companies' scale. Airbus announced it will appeal to the Court of Cassation, France's highest criminal court.

Why it matters: The verdict carries legal significance on multiple levels. It reestablishes that aviation manufacturers and carriers can face criminal liability for systemic failures when they knowingly allow defects and training gaps to persist. France's successful appellate reversal of a corporate criminal acquittal is rare and sets a precedent for future major-disaster prosecutions. For global airworthiness regulators, the finding that Airbus bore criminal responsibility for pitot tube deficiencies — even after EASA and FAA mandated replacements post-crash — raises questions about whether post-hoc regulatory compliance is sufficient to defeat criminal liability when the manufacturer knew of the risk before the accident. Families of the 228 victims have pursued accountability for 17 years; the ruling delivers criminal recognition that no civil settlement could provide. Airbus's Court of Cassation challenge will focus on legal and procedural questions rather than factual findings, meaning the core liability determination is likely to stand regardless of outcome.

Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin signed a broad digital-sovereignty agreement at their May 2026 Beijing summit covering joint AI governance, GLONASS-BeiDou satellite navigation interoperability, internet sovereignty coordination, and shared open-source software development to reduce Western technology dependence.

The May 2026 Beijing summit produced formal technology commitments with major security implications. On navigation, Russia and China agreed to coordinate GLONASS and BeiDou satellite systems, improve interoperability, and collaborate on radio frequency allocation, satellite orbits, and IoT integration — directly upgrading Russia's precision targeting capabilities with higher-accuracy Chinese systems independent of US GPS. On AI, China proposed a global AI cooperation organization; both nations jointly opposed using AI "as a geopolitical tool" for technological dominance, framing their programs as defensive responses to Western pressure. Ukraine has documented Russian use of AI-embedded malware in active cyberwarfare operations. On cyberspace, both nations committed to "internet sovereignty" — the doctrine that governments should control domestic digital environments — and agreed to share experience in content regulation and platform governance, a framework directly opposed to the open internet model promoted by the US and EU. Both nations are also accelerating joint open-source software development to substitute for Western technology stacks blocked by sanctions and export controls.

Why it matters: The pact formalizes an alignment between the world's most sophisticated AI and satellite infrastructure (China) and a nation that has demonstrated willingness to weaponize cyberspace in kinetic conflict (Russia). GLONASS-BeiDou interoperability directly enhances Russia's military precision guidance in Ukraine and future conflicts, providing Chinese-calibrated accuracy that Western sanctions and GPS jamming were intended to deny. The internet sovereignty framework is equally consequential over the longer term: both nations are investing heavily in Global South digital infrastructure, and their coordinated promotion of sovereignty-based governance through shared technical standards and capacity-building has the potential to entrench government-controlled internet architectures in dozens of developing countries before democratic alternatives can gain traction. For US and European export control strategists, the joint open-source commitment signals the coalition is explicitly working to reduce the leverage that technology restrictions provide — accelerating the trajectory toward a bifurcated global technology ecosystem from theoretical to operational. Western intelligence agencies have consistently identified this China-Russia technology alignment as among their highest-priority long-term threat concerns.

entry.title: [tech law] UK cybercrime law reform would protect only 300 of Britain's 70,000 security researchers, experts warn
entry.summary: The UK government's long-awaited amendment to the Computer Misuse Act 1990 would restrict its statutory defense to roughly 300 accredited professionals — 0.4 percent of the country's 70,000-strong cybersecurity workforce — while barring them from verifying whether a discovered vulnerability is genuine.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The UK government's long-awaited amendment to the Computer Misuse Act 1990 would restrict its statutory defense to roughly 300 accredited professionals — 0.4 percent of the country's 70,000-strong cybersecurity workforce — while barring them from verifying whether a discovered vulnerability is genuine.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis announced plans to amend the Computer Misuse Act 1990 following years of industry pressure. The proposed statutory defense is narrow in ways experts say make it functionally useless. Protection covers only scanning internet-facing systems; researchers must stop immediately upon discovering a vulnerability — before confirming whether it is real or assessing its severity — the precise step most system owners require before taking remediation action. The defense is restricted to British nationals holding UK Cyber Security Council accreditation; accredited individuals must conduct tests personally without delegating to junior staff or automated tools. Approximately 300 people hold the required certification against a cybersecurity workforce of 70,000 — 0.4 percent of the sector. Cyber policy consultant Jen Ellis described "a misalignment between expectations and reality" and called the proposal "much narrower" than industry sought. Agentic AI scanning tools, now widely deployed across the sector, remain in a legal grey area, and the accreditation model excludes bug bounty hunters, academic researchers, hobbyists, and professionals at smaller firms.

Why it matters: The UK's reform places Britain below Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, and the United States — all of which have broader frameworks that do not require government certification and do not bar researchers from confirming vulnerabilities are real. The practical effect may be to worsen the UK's national security posture: if legitimate researchers cannot legally test and disclose vulnerabilities, those flaws remain unpatched and exploitable by foreign state actors and criminal groups. For UK-based technology companies, the discrepancy between UK and European legal protections means security teams performing industry-standard practices in UK offices may be committing an offence that would be lawful in Paris or Amsterdam. The failure to address agentic AI tools creates a chilling effect on automated vulnerability scanning precisely when such tools are becoming indispensable — an ironic outcome from a reform ostensibly designed to strengthen the UK's cybersecurity ecosystem. Prior UK Computer Misuse Act reform attempts have stalled for years under successive governments, and the industry's disappointment with this proposal makes another multi-year delay likely.

entry.title: [tech law] FTC issues first Take It Down Act enforcement letters to 12 major platforms including Meta, Google, and TikTok
entry.summary: The FTC sent warning letters to 12 major tech companies on May 20 for failing to comply with the Take It Down Act, which became enforceable May 19, 2026, requiring platforms to remove nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The FTC sent warning letters to 12 major tech companies on May 20 for failing to comply with the Take It Down Act, which became enforceable May 19, 2026, requiring platforms to remove nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours.

The Take It Down Act (TIDA), enacted in May 2025 and enforceable as of May 19, 2026, requires online platforms to provide victims with a process to request removal of nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) — including AI-generated deepfakes — and to delete the flagged content within 48 hours of receiving a request. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson dispatched warning letters to Alphabet (Google/YouTube), Amazon, Apple, Automattic (WordPress), Bumble, Discord, Match Group, Meta, Microsoft, Pinterest, Reddit, SmugMug, Snapchat, TikTok, and X for failing to meet the law's requirements. The FTC's letters urged each company to implement photo-hashing technology to detect and remove duplicate images simultaneously, share hashes with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children for minor images and with StopNCII.org for adult images, display clear TIDA compliance notices on their homepages, allow victims to submit removal requests directly from images, and provide tracking numbers so victims can monitor the status of removal requests. Non-compliance carries civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation. Ferguson stated the FTC stands "ready to monitor compliance, investigate violations, and enforce the Take It Down Act," signaling that these letters are a warning, not the final enforcement action.

Why it matters: This is the first major regulatory salvo under TIDA and marks a significant moment in platform governance for intimate-image abuse: after years of voluntary compliance programs producing inconsistent results, federal law now mandates enforceable timelines and specific technical mechanisms. The 48-hour removal window is the shortest mandatory response time yet imposed on US platforms for any category of content, and the $53,088 per-violation penalty structure creates a strong financial incentive to build robust automated detection rather than rely on manual review queues. The cross-platform hash-sharing requirement — channeled through NCMEC and StopNCII — creates a shared detection infrastructure that, if fully implemented, would significantly raise the floor for all covered platforms simultaneously. For major AI companies developing generative image tools, this enforcement posture means the FTC is unlikely to treat image-generation products as exempt from TIDA just because they don't host images long-term. EU-based observers note that TIDA's architecture mirrors elements of the DSA's mandatory content-detection provisions, suggesting converging regulatory standards on both sides of the Atlantic.
